stimulus.body: The working note below records the evidence for a claim about tracing a semitone chain through a melody. c to E flat is three semitones and E flat to G is four more, giving seven total. A marginal reminder adds: add the steps between consecutive notes. A reader must decide which of the four proposed statements the note warrants, without using outside knowledge.

questions.stem: Read this item with “Trace a semitone chain through a melody / Add the steps between consecutive notes. / Tracing a semitone chain through a melody” as the standard. Which choice qualifies?
questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: c to E flat is three semitones and E flat to G is four more, giving seven total. On that basis "Seven semitones, the correct total" is the supported choice. Option A ("Six semitones, stopping short") fails because it stops one step short; Option D ("Eight semitones, adding an extra") fails because it adds an extra semitone; Option C ("Five semitones, confusing with five") fails because it confuses with a five-semitone span.
questions.hint: Add the steps between consecutive notes.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Scientific pitch notation and middle C
questions.learningObjective: Explain scientific pitch notation and middle C

stimulus.body: A short reference note on scientific pitch notation and middle c is set for a close-reading task. It states: Octave numbers increase as pitch rises, so notes just above middle C remain in octave four until C5, which begins octave five. A marginal reminder adds: middle C is C4. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The prompt gives “Explain scientific pitch notation and middle C / Middle C is C4. / Scientific pitch notation and middle C” as the nudge. Which option is really supported?

answer.exemplar: Octave numbers increase as pitch rises, so notes just above middle C remain in octave four until C5, which begins octave five.

questions.explanation: Octave numbers increase as pitch rises, so notes just above middle C remain in octave four until C5, which begins octave five. The number does not change at middle C itself.
